facts.claim: UNESCO inscribed 'Fado, urban popular song of Portugal' on the Representative List of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity in 2011 (6.COM). UNESCO describes it as a performance genre of music and poetry widely practised by communities in Lisbon, usually a solo singer accompanied by a wire-strung acoustic guitar and the Portuguese guitarra, performed professionally in concerts and small 'Fado houses' and by amateurs in older Lisbon neighbourhoods. The UNESCO text does NOT mention weddings or celebrations; frame Fado as music couples may choose, not as a wedding tradition.
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/fado-urban-popular-song-of-portugal-00563 (page title: 'Fado, urban popular song of Portugal - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage', HTTP 200)

facts.claim: UNESCO inscribed 'Cante Alentejano, polyphonic singing from Alentejo, southern Portugal' in 2014 (9.COM). UNESCO describes it as traditional two-part singing by amateur choral groups, performed without instruments, and says cante is 'a fundamental aspect of social life throughout Alentejano communities, permeating social gatherings in both public and private spaces'. UNESCO links it to social gatherings, not specifically to weddings.
facts.source: https://ich.unesco.org/en/RL/cante-alentejano-polyphonic-singing-from-alentejo-southern-portugal-01007 (page title: 'Cante Alentejano, polyphonic singing from Alentejo, southern Portugal - UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage', HTTP 200)

facts.claim: Priberam dictionary: 'copo-d'água' is the same as 'copo-de-água', defined as a meal of sweets and liqueurs offered to visitors or guests at a solemn occasion ('Refeição de doces e licores com que se obsequiam os visitantes ou os convidados de um acto solene'). Use as the Portuguese term for the reception after a wedding; do not claim the dictionary says 'wedding' specifically.

Australian Embassy Lisbon: Australians marrying in Portugal must contact the Portuguese Civil Registry office (Registo Civil) in the area where they intend to marry for the requirements; the embassy suggests rechecking requirements because they are subject to change by local authorities, and notes enquiries are best sent in Portuguese.

Australian Embassy Lisbon lists what is needed to marry in Portugal: an original birth certificate issued within six months, with a translation into Portuguese; an Australian passport (or Portuguese residency card if resident); and a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI). It states all documents must have at least six months validity.

Australian Embassy Lisbon: processing takes a minimum of four weeks and, once approved, the marriage must occur within a three-month period. CONFLICT: the Portuguese Justice portal says couples have up to six months to marry once authorised (fact_109).
facts.conflicts: Embassy: marry within 3 months of approval. justica.gov.pt (updated 28.07.2026): up to 6 months. Copy should not state a window; say 'check the validity period with the registry office'.

facts.claim: Australian Embassy Lisbon issues the Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage. Applicants complete an application form witnessed by a Consular Officer or a local notary public and present a current Australian passport (or Australian birth certificate plus photo ID), original divorce papers (Decree Absolute) if previously married, a death certificate if widowed, the partner's original identification, and payment of the fee. In-person lodgement is by appointment; lodgement by post is possible with notarised copies. The embassy says the current notarial service fee applies (a fee applies; amount not stated in copy).

Australian Embassy Lisbon: if original divorce papers must be submitted to Portuguese authorities, they may need an Apostille of the Hague; the embassy can provide an Apostille by appointment. The embassy also says an Australian visiting Portugal and marrying an Australian or a non-Portuguese resident should contact the Portuguese Civil Registry Office or seek an English-speaking lawyer to assist.

Portuguese Justice portal (justica.gov.pt, IRN as responsible body, updated 28.07.2026): the marriage process (processo de casamento) can be for a civil, Catholic, or civil-in-religious-form marriage, and begins with a declaration of the intention to marry (declaração da vontade de casar) at a civil registry office (conservatória do registo civil). Couples should organise the process at least one month before the chosen date. Foreigners present a residence permit, passport or equivalent document. Couples state the type of marriage, place, property regime (regime de bens), and date and time.

Portuguese Justice portal: between the start of the process and the wedding anyone may raise impediments at the registry office; once the marriage is authorised the couple has up to six months to marry. The process can be started by the couple or by a representative with a power of attorney with special powers (procuração). Online start is only for Portuguese citizens (or Brazilians with equal-rights status) with Chave Móvel Digital or Cartão de Cidadão, so Australians start in person or through a representative.

Portuguese Justice portal states the marriage process and registration cost 120 euros, with possible additional costs, for example to marry on a weekend or public holiday or to make a prenuptial agreement. PRICE: per brief, copy says only 'a fee applies, with extra costs for weekend or public-holiday weddings'; no amount in copy without Nic's sign-off.

IRN 'Organizar o casamento' (updated 28.07.2026), section 'Casar em Portugal para cidadãos estrangeiros': foreign couples who want to marry in Portugal go to a Registo Civil (civil registry office) to start the marriage process and present identification documents, a birth certificate issued under the law of their country, and a certificate of capacity to marry (certificado de capacidade matrimonial) issued by their country's competent authorities less than six months earlier (or a declaration that such a certificate is not issued). Certificates and documents not written in English, French or Spanish need a certified translation into Portuguese. If the foreign partner does not speak Portuguese and the registry officer does not speak their language, an interpreter is appointed.
facts.conflicts: Translation: IRN says documents in English need no translation; the Australian Embassy page (fact_104) says the birth certificate should be accompanied by a Portuguese translation. Copy: 'check with the registry office whether a certified Portuguese translation is needed'.

facts.claim: IRN: the marriage process starts with a declaration for marriage stating the type (civil, Catholic, or civil in religious form), the place, and the property regime. It can be started by the couple, by representatives with special powers, or by the parish priest or minister of a religious community established in Portugal, on request. Once the marriage is authorised, the couple has up to six months to marry. If no property regime is chosen, the default is comunhão de adquiridos (community of acquired property).

IRN: date, time and place of the civil wedding are agreed with the registrar (conservador/a). A civil wedding can take place at a registry office in normal hours; to marry elsewhere or outside normal hours, including weekends and public holidays, the date and time must be agreed beforehand with the registrar. On the day, the couple (or one partner and the other's representative) must be present; two to four witnesses may take part but are not compulsory; anyone may attend. In Lisbon and the Algarve, public municipal spaces are available for weddings: Câmara Municipal de Lisboa and Câmara Municipal de Albufeira.

IRN fee table: marrying at the civil registry costs 120 euros; a non-urgent wedding outside the registry office, or at the registry outside opening hours or on a Saturday, Sunday or public holiday, is listed at 200 euros; prenuptial agreements 100 or 160 euros. PRICE: copy should say 'a fee applies, with higher fees for weddings outside the registry office or on weekends and public holidays' unless Nic signs off figures.

Smartraveller (DFAT), 'How to get a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage', last updated 01/10/2026: a CNI is a DFAT document issued in support of an intended marriage overseas, issued through Australian Passport Offices, overseas embassies and consulates, or by mail. DFAT charges fees (indexed to CPI each 1 January). At least one applicant must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident. DFAT cannot advise on another country's legal processes; couples should confirm whether they need a CNI, whether it must be issued in the country of marriage, and whether it needs an apostille. Supporting documents not in English need a professional English translation.

Diário da República, 1.ª série, N.º 105, 31 May 2010: Lei n.º 9/2010 'Permite o casamento civil entre pessoas do mesmo sexo' (permits civil marriage between people of the same sex), approved 11 February 2010, promulgated 17 May 2010, published 31 May 2010. Copy: 'Same-sex civil marriage has been legal in Portugal since 2010 (Law 9/2010)'. Do not say 'one of the first countries'.

Smartraveller 'Getting married overseas' (last updated 18/08/2026): you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it happened and would have been valid under Australian law. A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of marriage but may not work as proof of a name change; check with your state or territory births, deaths and marriages registry and talk to a lawyer to confirm validity. Australia does not recognise overseas marriages where a party is already married, under age, too closely related or forced.

Smartraveller Portugal (re-used from 02-research/pages/smartraveller.md; page updated 16 October 2026, still current 03 November 2026): Australian Embassy Lisbon (Avenida da Liberdade 200) requires an appointment for passport and notarial services, booked via the embassy website; Portuguese government English pages are 'often out of date or inaccurate', so contact the Portuguese embassy or consulate for current information.

Smartraveller Portugal (re-used): overall level 'Exercise normal safety precautions', no higher-level areas; high summer temperatures and bushfires regularly affect mainland Portugal including coastal and tourist areas; falling rocks and cliff erosion in the Algarve; EES biometric registration on arrival may cause border delays, especially at Lisbon airport; dual nationality recognised and dual nationals should check which passport to use.

SEARCH-SUMMARY-ONLY (not a fetched page): editorial food sources in search results describe caldo verde as a potato and kale (or collard) soup from northern Portugal, often served with chouriço or linguiça (Serious Eats snippet: 'a potato and kale soup from northern Portugal'). No official or Visit Portugal page fetched in time (visitportugal.com/en/content/caldo-verde fetch failed). Its place late in the wedding night is NOT sourced: frame as 'often'.

SEARCH-SUMMARY-ONLY: Portuguese-language search results for the groom's tie cut and sold to guests are almost entirely Brazilian sites; one Brazilian bridal magazine snippet calls the tie-cutting custom 'de origem bem brasileira' (of Brazilian origin). No Portuguese official, museum or encyclopaedia source found. Present only as 'often told, and shared with Brazilian weddings' or drop.

facts.conflicts: Brief treats the tie as a Portuguese custom; search snippets attribute it to Brazil. Not resolved; 'often told' framing only.

insider_details.detail: Start the paperwork early: the Portuguese registry asks couples to open the marriage process at least a month before the date, and the Australian Embassy says processing takes at least four weeks, so lodge it well ahead of the date and plan around the validity period.

Australians cannot start the process online (that is limited to Portuguese citizens with digital ID), so it happens in person at a Conservatória do Registo Civil or through a representative holding a power of attorney with special powers; many couples who live in Australia use the second route.

Book the CNI appointment at the Australian Embassy in Lisbon early, or lodge by post with notarised copies; the IRN wants the certificate of capacity issued within six months of lodging, so time it close to the date.

A wedding outside the registry office, after hours, or on a weekend or public holiday must be agreed with the conservador in advance and attracts a higher official fee, which matters for a Saturday celebration at a quinta.
Witnesses are optional at a Portuguese civil wedding (two to four may take part), and an interpreter is appointed if needed, so padrinhos can be honoured without it being a legal requirement.

For summer outdoor ceremonies, plan shade, water and a heat or bushfire contingency, and keep clifftop Algarve photos well back from edges; allow extra arrival time at Lisbon airport for guests because of EES border checks.
